Photograph: Vahid Salemi/AP Iran High-level delegation visits Iran to try to avert flare-up with US and Israel Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey travel to Tehran as bellicose rhetoric heightens Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.03 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google High-level diplomatic delegations from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent renewed fighting between Iran and the US and Israel as rhetoric sharpens on both sides . Security officials and diplomats at Monday’s meeting were expected to discuss how Iran could persuade the Houthis in Yemen to end their crippling missile and drone attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia . With fighting raging across Yemen, the Houthis claimed to have closed Riyadh airport and inflicted heavy damage on the Saudi economy. The officials were also understood to be discussing Iran’s possible inclusion in a new security pact involving Islamic countries. The Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, Ibrahim Kalın, were to meet Iran’s top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington. The three countries signed a defence agreement in Mecca in August. Some in Iran feared the deal was constructed to challenge Tehran, but the signatory countries have insisted it is simply a mutual defence pact. The balance between exploring a new long-term security architecture and demanding Iran start to compromise in the conflicts in which it is engaged will be critical. It is possible the two sides came to the meeting with different priorities. View image in fullscreen The Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, meeting Pakistan’s Field Marshal Asim Munir in Riyadh in September. Photograph: Saudi Press Agency/Reuters The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role, and the US-Iran conflict has potentially reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran. No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attack on Iran either last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said the meeting could pave the way for broader regional cooperation on security based on shared interest. Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks Read more “The events of the last two years, especially the past eight months, have shown that sustainable and reliable security in our region will only be possible by building trust and cooperation among the countries of the region,” he said. Javad Zarif, a former foreign minister and long-term advocate of a regional security alliance called for “a comprehensive regional network based on non-aggression, mutual trust building, and shared prosperity”. “Regional security is not imported, it must be created by the people of this very region together,” he said. He published his message alongside an image of verses 103 and 159 from Surah Ali ‘Imran, the third chapter of the Qur’an. The verses emphasise being saved from a fiery pit by avoiding division, fostering unity, seeking forgiveness and consulting others. The meeting takes place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators, it was confirmed, spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz. Israeli media reports claimed the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday. Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that modern-day US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity in the region. The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners also increasingly argue Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb, ending the fatwa on the possession of a weapon of mass destruction. A pact likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters Cybercrime Analysis Cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers has geopolitical context Dan Milmo Global technology editor ‘Not particularly complex’ defrosting hack has been attributed to Iran, with presumption it is linked to others across Europe Mon 9 Nov 2026 14.40 EST Last modified on Mon 9 Nov 2026 14.42 EST Share Iranian hackers like to send a message. In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm. Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment. There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. ‌In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers. France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible. View image in fullscreen An employee fills boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyber-attack. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters It follows attacks on industrial freezers at an Israeli food production plant in May and a wave of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at US military bases in August that are now reportedly being treated as a suspected hack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? Read more Rafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said. Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked. Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies. View image in fullscreen Boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyber-attack. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic? Read more “In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said. The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. The main concern is AI, a technology now capable of highlighting previously unforeseen flaws in IT systems and helping attackers plan and carry out attacks. However, the underlying context of the fridge attacks is not AI but geopolitics. After all, the refrigeration system vulnerabilities were relatively easy to find and exploit. But a combination of groundbreaking technology and tense global relations makes for an alarming landscape. https://24.hu/kulfold/2026/11/09/orosz-v.text: Több mint 400 ezer orosz katona haláláról árulkodhat egy, az orosz statisztikai hivatalból, a Roszstatból kiszivárgott adatbázis, amelyet a Guardian és más nemzetközi sajtóorgánumok is megvizsgáltak . A belarusz kötődésű Cyber Partisans és az ukrán Silent Crow hekkercsoport által megszerzett állomány több mint 11 millió halotti anyakönyvi kivonat adatait tartalmazza. Az elemzés szerint 412 576 halálesetnél szerepel közvetlen utalás az ukrajnai háborúra vagy katonai műveletekre. A Guardian megjegyzi, hogy a teljes adatbázis hitelességét nem tudta függetlenül ellenőrizni, ugyanakkor a számok összhangban vannak más becslésekkel. A brit hírszerzés szeptemberben mintegy 500 ezer halott orosz katonáról beszélt, míg az orosz független Mediazona közel 286 ezer elesett katona nevét azonosította nyilvános források alapján. A lap szerint a tényleges veszteség szintén félmillió körül lehet. Janis Kluge , a berlini Nemzetközi és Biztonsági Ügyek Intézetének szakértője szerint a kiszivárgott adatok hitelesnek tűnnek, ugyanakkor a valós szám még magasabb lehet, mert sok eltűnt vagy azonosítatlan katona nem szerepel a nyilvántartásban. Az adatok szerint az orosz veszteségek területileg is egyenlőtlenül oszlanak meg. Burjátföldön, Tuva köztársaságban és a Bajkálontúli határterületen a háborús halálesetek az összes, 18 és 49 év közötti férfi halálozásának mintegy harmadát adták a vizsgált időszakban. Moszkvában és Szentpéterváron ugyanez az arány körülbelül 10 százalék volt. A kiszivárgott adatok arra is utalnak, hogy a harctéri veszteségek a háború elhúzódásával nőttek. Egyes hónapokban 15 ezer fölé emelkedhetett az elesett orosz katonák száma, ami napi átlagban mintegy 500 halottat jelent. A jelentés szerint ez jól mutatja, hogy a közel öt éve tartó háború emberi áldozatai továbbra is rendkívül magasak, miközben a béketárgyalások ellenére egyelőre nem látszik a konfliktus vége.
